analysis.one_liner: Imposes federal limits on product-injury lawsuits, capping punitive damages and shielding implant-material suppliers.
analysis.headline: The Senate Commerce Committee approved the bill in April 1995 with a bipartisan 20-sponsor roster, but it sat on the Senate calendar for 20 months and never received a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have replaced the differing state rules for lawsuits over defective products with a single federal set of rules. It would have capped punitive damages at three times the financial loss or $250,000 (whichever is greater), set a two-year deadline for filing and a 20-year cutoff for durable goods, and made each defendant pay only its own share of pain-and-suffering damages. It also would have largely exempted companies that supply raw materials for medical implants from lawsuits over implant injuries, and given workers' compensation insurers new rights to take part of injury settlements.
analysis.who_benefits: Product manufacturers, retailers and sellers, their liability insurers, and suppliers of raw materials for medical implants. The bill would cap their punitive-damage exposure, shorten the window for suing them, make it harder to hold stores and distributors liable, end joint liability for pain-and-suffering awards, and largely exempt biomaterials suppliers from implant-injury lawsuits. Workers' compensation insurers would also gain new rights to recover benefits from settlements.

how_it_helps.text: Caps punitive damages at three times the compensatory economic loss or $250,000, whichever is greater, and requires proof of 'conscious, flagrant indifference to the safety of others' by clear and convincing evidence — a much higher bar than ordinary proof.
Sets a two-year deadline for filing suit from the date of discovery and a 20-year cutoff on claims involving durable goods, replacing longer state-law periods in some states.

Makes stores, distributors, and lessors liable only if they were negligent, broke their own express warranty, or engaged in intentional wrongdoing — rather than being strictly liable for selling a defective product.
Ends joint liability for noneconomic (pain-and-suffering) damages, so each defendant pays only its allocated percentage and no defendant can be made to cover an unpayable co-defendant's share.

Gives biomaterials suppliers a near-complete defense in implant lawsuits unless they manufactured the device, resold it, or supplied materials that failed contract specifications — with special fast-track procedures to dismiss claims against them.
Gives workers' compensation insurers a right of subrogation to recover benefits from settlements and judgments, and blocks an injured worker from settling without the insurer's written consent.
Overrides inconsistent state rules on the issues it covers, giving manufacturers a single national litigation rulebook instead of fifty different ones.

analysis.who_pays: People injured or killed by defective products, who would face shorter deadlines to sue, capped punitive damages, harder cases against retailers, no joint liability for pain-and-suffering awards, and a near-shield for the companies that supply implant materials. Workers injured on the job could also see part of any settlement diverted to their workers' compensation insurer.

drawbacks.text: Punitive damages — the penalty for knowingly dangerous conduct — would be capped at three times economic loss or $250,000, with a high 'conscious, flagrant indifference' proof standard, and the court would apply the cap without telling the jury what the true limit is.

The two-year filing deadline and 20-year cutoff for durable goods would override longer deadlines in some states, cutting off valid claims from people who learn of harm late or are injured by long-lived products.

Ending joint liability for pain-and-suffering damages means an injured person absorbs the shortfall whenever one responsible defendant is bankrupt, unknown, or immune — a shift from companies to victims.

The biomaterials title would bar most lawsuits against the companies that supply raw materials and components inside medical implants, leaving patients harmed by a defective implant to sue only the device maker even when a supplier's substandard material caused the failure.

The workers' compensation subrogation provisions would let insurers intercept part of an injured worker's settlement and would require the insurer's written consent before the worker could settle at all.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had a genuine argument behind it: a patchwork of 50 state liability regimes raises costs, and Congress's own findings in the bill state that implant-material suppliers had stopped supplying materials because defending lawsuits cost far more than their sales to device makers, threatening the availability of lifesaving devices [S4]. Its defenders would also note real claimant-side features, such as making a seller liable as a manufacturer when the true manufacturer can't be served or a judgment can't be enforced, a fee penalty on defendants who refuse mediation in bad faith, and carve-outs protecting workers whose employers are immune from suit [S4]. But the core of the bill runs the other way: it caps and shortens the remedies of people hurt by products — capped punitive damages, a two-year deadline, no joint liability, seller liability relaxed, suppliers shielded — while leaving the underlying safety incentives of state law weakened. The bill was reported with minority views filed, and it never got a floor debate or vote where that trade-off could be weighed.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Commerce Committee approved it and put it on the Senate's waiting list in April 1995, but no one ever brought it up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rockefeller introduced the bill on March 15, 1995, with 10 original cosponsors from both parties.
The Senate Consumer subcommittee held hearings on April 3 and 4, 1995.
The Commerce Committee ordered the bill reported favorably on April 6, 1995, and it was reported on April 18 with a substitute amendment and written report No. 104-69; minority views were filed.
The bill was placed on the Senate calendar (Calendar No. 91) on April 18, 1995, but no further action was ever taken, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People injured by defective products came out ahead: because the bill never became law, they kept the fuller protections and remedies of their state's product liability law. Manufacturers, sellers, and insurers gained nothing from the bill's proposed limits, though the broader tort-reform push of that era continued through other bills.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers kept their state-law lawsuit rights

sides.party_line_note: A Senate Democrat sponsored the bill with 16 Republican and 3 Democratic cosponsors, and the Commerce Committee reported it favorably — though minority views were filed — and the bill never reached a Senate vote, so the opposition's shape was never measured on a roll call.

industries.note: The bill would cap punitive damages, impose a two-year filing deadline and a 20-year cutoff for durable goods, and make each defendant pay only its own share of pain-and-suffering damages. Each provision shifts the cost of defective and dangerous products from the company that made or sold them to the person hurt by them.

The bill would give insurers a right to recover workers' compensation benefits from any settlement or judgment, and would bar an injured worker from settling without the insurer's written consent. That money would come out of what injured workers keep, though the bill also lets manufacturers shift blame onto immunized employers in exchange for paying the insurer's legal fees if the blame doesn't stick.

Title II would exempt biomaterials suppliers from implant-injury lawsuits unless they are the manufacturer, resold the finished implant, or delivered materials that failed contract specifications. Congress's stated findings were that litigation risk was driving suppliers out of the small implant-materials market and threatening the supply of lifesaving devices; the trade-off is that patients harmed by a defective implant would lose recourse against the companies that supplied the materials inside it.
Damage caps, shorter deadlines, and the near-immunity for biomaterials suppliers would shrink the pool of cases and recoveries that fund plaintiffs' contingency work.
